facts.source: IRC 2021 R905.7 / R905.8 (wood shingles and shakes)
facts.fact: Spaced (skip) sheathing, where boards are laid with gaps between them so the roofing can breathe and dry, is a permitted deck for wood shingle and wood shake roofs; most other roof coverings require solid sheathing.
Gutter runs are commonly limited so that the high point is no more than roughly 25 to 40 ft from a downspout; longer runs get a downspout at each end with the gutter pitched toward both.
facts.note: Card says 25 ft maximum from high point to downspout. This is a trade rule of thumb, not a code requirement, and published guidance varies (often 30-40 ft). Not exam-confirmed.

facts.fact: Face-frame wall and base cabinets are fastened to the wall by driving screws through the horizontal hanging (hang) rails at the back of the cabinet box into the wall studs.

In sawn-lumber floor joists, notches may not be placed in the middle one-third of the span; notches in the top or bottom edge elsewhere are limited to 1/6 of the joist depth and a length of 1/3 of the depth, and notches at the ends (bearing) are limited to 1/4 of the depth.

facts.source: Standard practice; IRC 2021 R609.4 / R703.4 (install per manufacturer)
facts.fact: Rough-opening sizes and installation details for a manufactured window such as an aluminum-clad wood unit come from the manufacturer's published data and installation instructions, which the code also requires to be followed.

facts.source: Cold-formed steel framing practice (AISI S240 / manufacturer details)
facts.fact: When cold-formed steel track must be spliced, a short piece of track or stud is nested inside and fastened so it laps each side of the joint; a minimum splice length of about 6 in is commonly cited.
facts.note: Card says 6 in minimum track splice. Splice details depend on the AISI standard, manufacturer and engineer's details; could not confirm a single code minimum.

facts.fact: A hopper window is hinged at the bottom and its top tilts inward into the room; the opposite type, hinged at the top with the bottom swinging outward, is an awning window.

facts.source: NWFA installation guidelines (wood flooring over wood subfloor)
facts.fact: Before nailing solid hardwood strip flooring such as oak over a clean wood subfloor, a common recommended step is to lay 15-lb asphalt-saturated felt (or an equivalent vapor retarder) with its seams overlapped.
Concrete flatwork is finished in this order: screed (strike off) to grade, bull float, wait for bleed water to leave, then edge and joint, float, and finally trowel.

Where roof trusses or rafters bear on an exterior wall top plate, the connection must resist wind uplift (and lateral thrust); when calculated uplift exceeds what toenails provide, approved connectors such as hurricane ties are required.

Exposed wiring where physical damage is expected should be run in a raceway rated for it, such as rigid metal conduit, IMC, or Schedule 80 PVC; armored cable (Type AC, often called BX) is not permitted where subject to physical damage.
facts.note: Card says BX (armored cable). NEC 320.12 prohibits Type AC cable where subject to physical damage; rigid/IMC conduit or Schedule 80 PVC is the correct choice (EMT is excluded only where damage is severe).

facts.fact: Before insulating an attic or ceiling, check recessed light fixtures: unless a fixture is rated Type IC for insulation contact, insulation must be kept at least 3 in from it and not placed over it.

facts.source: Standard construction practice; IRC 2021 R608 (ICF walls)
facts.fact: Insulating concrete forms (ICFs), hollow foam blocks or panels filled with reinforced concrete, are stay-in-place forms that remain as part of the finished wall and provide its insulation.
A window should sit loosely in its rough opening, which is made slightly larger than the unit, so it can be shimmed plumb, level and square without being forced or racked.

Wood flooring should be installed only after the building's HVAC is running and the space is held at normal living temperature and humidity, typically around 60-80 degrees F, so the wood is acclimated to in-service conditions.
facts.note: Card says 70 degrees F. Industry guidance gives a range of normal living conditions (temperature plus relative humidity) rather than a single temperature; exact ranges vary by guideline and manufacturer.

facts.fact: Foundation drains are typically perforated pipe laid with the holes facing down, surrounded by gravel or crushed stone that extends at least 1 ft beyond the footing and 6 in above its top, and wrapped or covered with a filter membrane.

Collar ties connecting opposing rafters must be in the upper third of the attic space, at least 1x4 nominal, and spaced no more than 4 ft on center, which is every third rafter pair when rafters are 16 in on center.
facts.note: Card says every fourth pair of rafters at 16 in o.c. That is 64 in apart; the IRC limits collar tie spacing to 4 ft o.c., i.e., every third pair at 16 in o.c.

facts.fact: The kraft paper facing on batt insulation serves as a vapor retarder (a Class II vapor retarder under the IRC) and is installed toward the warm-in-winter side of the wall.
Counterflashing is fastened to or set into the wall and turned down over the top edge of the base flashing, shedding water past that edge while letting the roof and wall move independently.
Material quantities for a bid are measured (taken off) from the construction drawings, with the specifications defining the required quality and type of each material.
Medium-density fiberboard (MDF) has a dense, uniform, grain-free face, which makes it a good choice where a smooth painted finish is needed, such as cabinet panels, trim and shelving.
Shear in a concrete beam causes diagonal tension cracking, which usually starts near the supports at about 45 degrees; stirrups (shear reinforcement) are placed to resist it.
An inch-pound rebar number is its nominal diameter in eighths of an inch, so a #4 bar is 1/2 in (0.50 in) and a #6 bar is 3/4 in (0.75 in) in diameter.
ACI 117 allows stirrup spacing to vary by about plus or minus 1 in, as long as the total number of stirrups is not reduced.
facts.note: Card says 1 inch. I believe this matches ACI 117, but tolerance tables have changed between editions and I cannot confirm the current wording.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: cash flow / financial management
facts.fact: A cumulative cash flow (S) curve that rises steeply at the start shows a front-loaded project, where much of the cost or billing falls early; cash flow projections are built by tying the schedule of values to the construction schedule.
The American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers (ASHRAE) publishes the main industry standards for commissioning and for testing, adjusting and balancing HVAC systems.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: job cost accounting
facts.fact: Job cost documentation has two main purposes: to feed cost data into the company's accounting system and to build up information that lets managers control each project's costs.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: project delivery methods
facts.fact: In agency construction management, the owner holds separate contracts with the designer, the contractor(s), and a construction manager who acts only as the owner's advisor and does not guarantee cost.
Final as-built records should include, along with marked-up as-built drawings, photographs of conditions, especially concealed work such as underground and in-wall utilities taken before cover-up.
Under the Unified Soil Classification System, sand is soil that passes the No. 4 sieve (4.75 mm) but is retained on the No. 200 sieve (0.075 mm); coarser is gravel and finer is silt or clay.

Presumptive allowable foundation pressures without a soil report are 12,000 psf for crystalline bedrock, 4,000 psf for sedimentary/foliated rock, 3,000 psf for sandy gravel or gravel (GW, GP), 2,000 psf for sands and silty or clayey sands and gravels, and 1,500 psf for clays and silts.

facts.source: Principles and Practices of Commercial Construction (NASCLA reference text)
facts.fact: A NASCLA reference textbook is reported to list dense silt as suitable for roughly 3,000 psf (about 140 kPa) of estimated foundation bearing pressure, which differs from the IBC presumptive value for silts.
facts.note: Cards 355 and 363 answer dense silt for 3,000 psf / 140 kPa. Under IBC/IRC presumptive values silts get only 1,500 psf and 3,000 psf is for gravel. The textbook table could not be confirmed; students should know both.

facts.source: Equipment productivity rule of thumb (Peurifoy, Construction Planning, Equipment and Methods)
facts.fact: A naturally aspirated (non-turbocharged) engine loses roughly 3% of its rated power for every 1,000 ft of elevation above sea level, which reduces equipment output on high-altitude jobs.
Expansive (clay) soils change volume with moisture, swelling when they get wet and shrinking as they dry, which can heave or crack foundations and slabs.
Excavated soil swells in volume: typical published swell from bank to loose condition is about 10-15% for sand and gravel, about 20-25% for loam or common earth, and about 25-40% for clay.
facts.note: Cards say loam 20% and excavated clay 25%. Swell percentages vary by table and material condition; values are approximate and not code-based.

facts.fact: Where a sidewalk bears against a building or other fixed structure, isolation/expansion joints are provided there and at intervals along the walk, commonly cited as no more than about 30 ft apart.
facts.note: Card says 30 ft maximum. This comes from a textbook or agency specification and varies by jurisdiction; not a model-code requirement.

facts.fact: Sheet piles are interlocking sections driven to form a wall that resists lateral (horizontal) earth and water pressure, as in cofferdams and excavation support; they are not intended to carry vertical building loads.

facts.source: Principles and Practices of Commercial Construction (metal panel systems)
facts.fact: Metal wall or roof panels designed as stressed-skin panels need no separate subframe and are attached directly to the building's structural frame, reportedly by clips.
facts.note: Card says clips. Attachment method depends on the panel system (clips or through-fasteners); could not confirm the textbook source.

facts.fact: In a pre-engineered metal building, rigid frames give stability across the width (transverse), while diagonal rod or cable (X) bracing in the roof and sidewalls gives longitudinal stability.
For gypsum-based plasters such as vermiculite plaster, the space is commonly held at 55 degrees F or above for about a week before, during, and after application until the plaster sets and dries.
facts.note: Card says 55 degrees F for a week before, during and after. This matches some manufacturer handbook guidance, but ASTM and other sources use different minimums (e.g., 40 degrees F); handbook-dependent.

facts.source: RSMeans square foot / assemblies cost data (area modifier method)
facts.fact: RSMeans square-foot costs are adjusted for building size by comparing the proposed area to the typical size for that building type; a project larger than typical gets a cost multiplier below 1.0 and a smaller one gets a multiplier above 1.0.
Value engineering seeks the required function and quality at the lowest life-cycle cost. It can happen at any stage, but the most savings come early in design, when changes are cheapest to make.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: estimating (general conditions)
facts.fact: General conditions costs such as supervision, the field office, and temporary utilities depend on time and are usually spread evenly across the project duration.

Submittals (shop drawings, product data sheets, and samples) are sent by the contractor to the designer to confirm that the proposed materials and products meet the contract documents; product data sheets show manufacturer specifications.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: labor estimating
facts.fact: Labor cost for a task is based on quantity, crew make-up and wage rates, and productivity (output per hour) under the job conditions; the logic links between activities affect the schedule, not the labor cost of the task.
Shoring may be removed only after the structure has enough strength to carry its loads, shown by tests of field-cured cylinders or another approved method of estimating in-place strength.
Concrete must be kept above 50 degrees F and moist for at least the first 7 days after placement, or at least the first 3 days for high-early-strength concrete, unless accelerated curing is used.
In beams of special (seismic) moment frames, hoops are required near each end of the beam, and the first hoop must be no more than 2 in from the face of the supporting column.
facts.note: Card asks about a column connected to a wall. The 2-in first-hoop rule in ACI 318 applies to beams framing into a supporting column in special moment frames.

facts.fact: A typical square or rectangular spread footing is a slab of uniform thickness with its main reinforcing bars near the bottom (tension) face, running in both directions.

Formwork for an elevated slab is designed for the slab's dead load plus a construction live load of at least 50 psf (75 psf if motorized carts are used), and the combined design load must be at least 100 psf (125 psf with motorized carts).
Field and lab quality-control tests on concrete follow ASTM standards: slump (C143), air content (C231 or C173), making and testing strength cylinders (C31 and C39), and unit weight and yield (C138).

facts.source: PCA Design and Control of Concrete Mixtures (air entrainment)
facts.fact: Entrained air improves freeze-thaw resistance, but too much air lowers compressive strength (roughly 5% per extra percentage point of air), so air content is held within the specified range.
Camber is building formwork slightly upward so that when wet concrete loads it and the forms deflect, the finished member ends up at the intended elevation.
Duplex (double-headed) nails are used for temporary work such as form bracing because the upper head stays exposed and can be pulled easily when the forms are stripped.
Lateral pressure on wall and column forms goes up with faster placement, deeper lifts, cooler concrete and retarded mixes, so slowing the rate of placement is the main field method of reducing it.

facts.source: ACI 306R cold weather concreting; ACI 318 chloride limits
facts.fact: In cold weather an accelerating admixture is added to speed setting and early strength; calcium chloride is the traditional accelerator (generally no more than 2% by weight of cement), but it is limited or prohibited in reinforced, prestressed, or aluminum-embedded concrete because chlorides cause corrosion.
Lightly dampening a dry subgrade before placing concrete stops it from quickly drawing mixing water out of the concrete; there should be no standing water or mud.

facts.source: ACI 305R hot weather concreting; ACI 232 fly ash
facts.fact: Replacing part of the cement with fly ash lowers and slows the heat of hydration, which helps in hot weather and mass pours; usual hot-weather measures also include retarders, chilled water or ice, and never adding water to the mix.
facts.note: Card says fly ash is used to cool concrete that contains too much water. Fly ash reduces heat of hydration; it is not a remedy for excess water, which lowers strength and must be prevented.

facts.fact: A set-retarding admixture slows setting so that hot concrete stays workable long enough to place and finish properly.
Admixtures are used for things like controlling set time, reducing water, entraining air and improving workability and durability; they are used to decrease permeability, never to increase it.
Higher concrete temperature shortens setting and finishing time sharply; one cited rule of thumb is that a 20 degree F increase cuts finishing time by about half.
facts.note: Card says a 20 degree F increase reduces finishing time by 50%. Published rules of thumb vary (some say about one-third per 20 degrees F); could not confirm the exact ACI figure.

facts.source: Fiber tube column form manufacturer guidance
facts.fact: Laminated fiber (cardboard tube) column forms need external bracing to stay plumb, with one cited threshold being forms taller than about 15 ft.
facts.note: Card says brace if over 15 ft. Bracing requirements come from manufacturer instructions and vary by diameter and conditions.

facts.source: ASTM C494 Types F and G
facts.fact: High-range water-reducing admixtures (superplasticizers) greatly increase slump without extra water, or allow large water reductions for high-strength concrete.
Gang forms are large panels assembled from smaller ones and moved by crane as a unit, which gives high reuse, covers large placements, and cuts erection time.
Contraction (control) joints in slabs on grade should be cut to at least one-quarter of the slab thickness, for example 1-1/4 in deep in a 5-in slab.

facts.source: SDI / AWS D1.3 (welding sheet steel deck)
facts.fact: Weld washers are required when arc spot (puddle) welding steel deck thinner than 0.028 in (about 22 gauge), because thin sheet would otherwise burn through.
Steel floor deck used as a working platform during construction must be able to support specified construction loads, with one cited minimum of 50 psf uniform.
facts.note: Card says 50 psf. SDI construction-load criteria (uniform and concentrated loads) vary by standard edition; could not confirm the exact figure.

facts.fact: A business owner's policy (BOP) packages commercial property and general liability coverage into one policy, usually for smaller businesses.
Umbrella liability insurance pays claims above the limits of underlying policies such as general liability, auto liability and employer's liability.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: estimating methods
facts.fact: Estimating methods range from conceptual (cost per square foot or per unit from past projects) to detailed quantity take-off. The square-foot method multiplies building area by a unit cost per square foot, while take-off prices each material and labor item one by one and is the most accurate.

Under AIA A201, unless the contract documents say otherwise, the contractor obtains and pays for the building permit and other government permits, fees, licenses and inspections needed to complete the work.
facts.note: Card says the owner is responsible for purchasing permits. Under the standard AIA A201 general conditions the contractor secures and pays for permits unless the contract assigns them elsewhere; responsibility is set by the contract.

facts.source: Contract law fundamentals (material vs. minor breach)
facts.fact: A minor breach, such as a payment that is one day late, lets the injured party recover damages but not stop performing. Walking off the job for good in response is itself a material breach, and a contract should be terminated only for a material breach.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: project documentation
facts.fact: Daily logs (job diaries) record weather, crews, work done and delays each day, and are the main evidence supporting a claim for a time extension such as for rain days.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: materials management
facts.fact: Just-in-time delivery schedules materials to arrive shortly before they are installed, which reduces the storage space needed on site and the risk of theft or damage.

facts.source: Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996; 42 USC 653a
facts.fact: Employers must report newly hired employees to their state's new-hire registry, and the data goes into the National Directory of New Hires, which is used mainly to locate parents and enforce child support orders.
Float (slack) is how long an activity can be delayed past its early start or finish without delaying the project completion date; critical-path activities have zero float.

A meal break counts as unpaid time only if the employee is fully relieved of duty. A non-exempt worker who must answer phones during a 30-minute clocked-out lunch is working, so in a week of five 8-hour days those 2.5 hours must be paid at 1.5 times the regular rate.

For non-exempt employees the FLSA requires records of hours worked each workday and each workweek, wages and pay data, but does not require any specific timekeeping method or a record of the clock time the employee left each day.

facts.source: USCIS Form I-9 Lists of Acceptable Documents
facts.fact: On Form I-9, an unrestricted Social Security card is a List C document: it proves employment authorization but not identity, so it must be paired with a List B identity document such as a driver's license.
Payments for services to an independent contractor who is a sole proprietor (not an employee) are reported on Form 1099-NEC; payments to corporations are generally exempt.
The OSHA 300 log, the 300A annual summary and the 301 incident reports must be kept for 5 years after the end of the calendar year they cover, with the 300 log updated during that period.
Under the Hazard Communication standard, employers must keep a Safety Data Sheet (SDS, formerly MSDS) for every hazardous chemical on site and make it readily available to workers during each shift.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: risk management and insurance
facts.fact: Insurance transfers the financial risk of losses such as accidents, theft, and property damage from the business to an insurer in return for a premium; property insurance in particular pays for physical loss or damage to owned buildings, contents and equipment.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: insurance (inland marine)
facts.fact: A contractor's equipment floater is an inland marine policy that covers direct physical loss to mobile tools and equipment wherever they are, whether in storage, in transit, or at a jobsite.
The employer pays workers' compensation insurance premiums and, in nearly all states, may not deduct them from employees' wages.

Under the cash method, revenue is recorded when it is received and expenses when they are paid. Under the accrual method, revenue is recorded when earned and expenses when incurred, whenever the cash actually moves.
A bar (Gantt) chart shows activity durations on a timeline, while a CPM schedule also shows the logical dependencies between activities, which lets it identify the critical path and float.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: contract types
facts.fact: Under a cost-plus contract, the monthly pay application bills the owner for the actual costs incurred, documented by records, plus the agreed fee, rather than a percentage of a fixed lump sum.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: project delivery methods
facts.fact: In design-build, the owner signs one contract with a single entity that is responsible for both design and construction and assembles the team of architects, engineers and builders.

Social Security tax is 6.2% of wages from the employee plus a matching 6.2% from the employer, up to the annual wage base. Medicare is 1.45% each with no wage cap, plus an extra 0.9% withheld from an employee's wages over $200,000.

facts.source: Family and Medical Leave Act, 29 CFR 825.110 and 825.112
facts.fact: FMLA gives eligible employees up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave in 12 months for birth of a child, adoption or foster placement, their own serious health condition, or caring for a spouse, child or parent with one. Eligibility requires 12 months of employment, 1,250 hours worked in the past 12 months, and 50 employees within 75 miles.

facts.source: CSI MasterFormat; NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: estimating
facts.fact: Estimates are easier to build and check when quantities and tasks are grouped by type of work, commonly following CSI MasterFormat divisions.
Both standard EIFS and EIFS with drainage must stop at least 6 in above the finished ground level.

EIFS insulation boards are set tightly together; gaps wider than about 1/16 in are filled with slivers of insulation, not base coat, and board joints are staggered and offset from sheathing joints and from the corners of openings.
facts.note: Cards say 1/16 in maximum gap and 6 in offset from sheathing joints and opening corners. These come from manufacturer instructions; offset distances differ by manufacturer (6-8 in).

facts.source: EIFS evaluation reports (ICC-ES AC219) / manufacturer specs
facts.fact: EIFS foam insulation board has a minimum thickness (commonly 3/4 in) and a maximum set by the system's evaluation report (commonly about 4 in).
facts.note: Card says maximum thickness 3/4 in; 3/4 in is usually cited as the MINIMUM. Limits are product-specific, so I did not mark this corrected.

facts.fact: EIFS reinforcing mesh must run continuously around corners and overlap adjoining mesh, including back-wrapped mesh, by a minimum commonly specified as 2-1/2 in.
facts.note: Cards 430 and 469 say 2-1/2 in. This is a manufacturer-handbook requirement, not a model-code provision.

facts.fact: In new Group R buildings, smoke alarms must get their primary power from the building wiring, with battery backup, and with no disconnecting switch other than the overcurrent protection.

In Types I and II construction, wood finish flooring may be attached to embedded or fireblocked wood sleepers, cemented to fire-resistance-rated construction, or attached to a wood subfloor on sleepers. Combustible insulating board beneath it is limited to 1/2 in thick, so 5/8-in board is not allowed.
A single hoistway enclosure may hold no more than four elevator cars, and where four or more cars serve the same part of a building they must be in at least two separate hoistways.
In Types I and II construction, skylight frames must be noncombustible, and skylights sloped less than 45 degrees from horizontal must sit on a curb at least 4 in above the roof plane.

Roof purlins are supported by 2x4 (minimum) struts running to bearing walls at a slope of at least 45 degrees from horizontal; struts may be at most 4 ft on center with an unbraced length of no more than 8 ft.
facts.note: Card says purlin struts shall not exceed 8 inches in length. The IRC limit is 8 FEET of unbraced strut length (with slope not less than 45 degrees).

facts.fact: Hand-held portable fire extinguishers must be mounted with at least 4 in of clearance between the floor and the bottom of the extinguisher; the top may be no higher than 5 ft for units of 40 lb or less, or 3-1/2 ft for heavier units.
Doors in fire-resistance-rated corridor walls need a fire protection rating of at least 20 minutes (1/3 hour) and must also meet smoke and draft control requirements.

Transom assemblies above doors in fire-resistance-rated walls must meet the rating requirements in IBC Section 716, which for some 2-hour assemblies call for fire-resistance-rated (not just fire-protection-rated) glazing.
facts.note: Card says a transom in a 2-hour exterior wall needs a 2-hour rating. Table 716.1(2) gives 1-1/2 hr for doors in 2-hr exterior walls, and transom rules depend on wall type and glazing; could not confirm the card's figure.

facts.fact: Stairways need at least 80 in (6 ft 8 in) of headroom, measured vertically from the line connecting the tread nosings; spiral stairs may have 78 in.
Smoke barriers generally need a 1-hour fire-resistance rating, but in Group I-3 (detention) buildings they may be built of steel sheet at least 0.10 in thick.
Footings must extend at least 12 in below undisturbed ground surface and also below the frost line unless they are frost-protected.
Combination subfloor-underlayment 3/4 in thick or less (including 5/8 in) is fastened to framing with 8d common nails or 6d deformed-shank nails, spaced 6 in at panel edges and 12 in in the field.
Valves controlling the water supply to automatic sprinkler systems, along with waterflow switches and other critical components, must be electrically supervised by a listed fire alarm control unit.
Where an elevator is required to have standby power and only one elevator is installed, it must transfer automatically to standby power within 60 seconds after normal power fails.

Shaft enclosures such as elevator hoistways must be rated 2 hours when they connect four or more stories and 1 hour when they connect fewer than four, and never less than the floor assembly they pass through.

Soil is classified as expansive when it meets all four criteria: plasticity index of 15 or more, more than 10% passing a No. 200 sieve, more than 10% of particles smaller than 5 micrometers, and an expansion index above 20. Testing the expansion index alone is allowed in place of the first three tests.

facts.source: IBC 2021 Section 803 (furred interior finish) and Section 718
facts.fact: Where wall or ceiling finish is set out from the structure on furring strips, the concealed space must be filled with noncombustible material or fireblocked at intervals of no more than 8 ft in any direction.
facts.note: Card says 8 inches. The IBC fireblocking interval for furred interior finish is 8 FEET in every direction.

facts.fact: Sill plates are anchored with at least 1/2-in bolts embedded at least 7 in into the concrete or grouted masonry, spaced no more than 6 ft apart, with a bolt within 12 in of each plate end and at least two per plate section.

Swinging doors serving a Group H occupancy must have panic or fire exit hardware whatever the occupant load. In Group A and E occupancies the requirement applies to rooms or spaces with an occupant load of 50 or more.
facts.note: Card says Group H doors need panic hardware at an occupant load of 50 or more. The 50-person threshold applies to Groups A and E; Group H requires panic or fire exit hardware with no occupant-load threshold.

facts.fact: On low-slope roofs (below 4:12) receiving photovoltaic or asphalt shingles, the IRC calls for a double-coverage underlayment application, with specified end laps that are staggered between courses (one cited figure is 4-in end laps offset 6 ft).
facts.note: Card says 4-in end laps offset 6 ft for slopes 3:12 to 4:12. Underlayment application tables and PV shingle slope limits changed between IRC editions; could not confirm the exact 2021 values.

facts.fact: In crawl spaces, wood joists or the underside of a wood structural floor closer than 18 in to exposed ground, and wood girders closer than 12 in, must be naturally durable or preservative-treated wood.
facts.note: Card says 13 in. The IRC thresholds are 18 in for floor joists and 12 in for girders above exposed ground in under-floor spaces.

facts.fact: On an accessible route, a change in level up to 1/4 in may be vertical; from 1/4 in to 1/2 in it must be beveled no steeper than 1:2; anything over 1/2 in must be ramped.
Accessible routes can be made up of walking surfaces with a running slope no steeper than 1:20, doorways, ramps, curb ramps (not counting flared sides), elevators and platform lifts.
A van-accessible parking space must be at least 132 in wide with a 60-in access aisle, or 96 in wide when the adjacent access aisle is at least 96 in wide.

Accessible washing machines need a clear floor space for a parallel approach centered on the appliance, and for front-loading machines one standard is cited as allowing the space's centerline to be offset up to 24 in from the door centerline.
facts.note: Card says 24 in maximum offset from the door centerline. ADA 611 centers the space on the appliance; the 24-in offset appears to come from an ICC A117.1 dwelling-unit provision that I could not confirm.

facts.fact: A ramp run with a rise greater than 6 in must have handrails on both sides, and handrails with a circular cross section must have an outside diameter of 1-1/4 in to 2 in.

In a wheelchair-accessible toilet compartment, the door goes in the front partition or the side wall farthest from the water closet; if it is in the front partition, the opening must be no more than 4 in from the side wall farthest from the toilet.
Accessible operable parts must work with one hand, without tight grasping, pinching or twisting of the wrist, and with no more than 5 lbf of force.
Accessible ramps may have a running slope no steeper than 1:12, and the cross slope of ramp runs and landings may be no steeper than 1:48, which still lets water drain without pooling.
For wheelchair users, a drinking fountain spout outlet may be no higher than 36 in above the floor; standing-person fountains have spouts 38 to 43 in high.
Manual control switches for automatic doors and gates must meet the operable-parts rules, and their clear floor space must be beyond the arc of the door swing.
A parapet is the part of a wall that extends above the roof deck; IBC 705.11 requires parapets on many exterior walls, generally at least 30 in high.

Guardrail systems need midrails, screens, mesh or equivalent intermediate members between the top rail and the walking/working surface wherever there is no wall or parapet at least 21 in high; midrails go midway, and the top rail is 42 in plus or minus 3 in.

facts.source: CRSI / AWS D1.4 guidance on tack welding reinforcing bars
facts.fact: Tack welding reinforcing bars (for example to hold bars in place) can seriously weaken them, so it is not allowed unless approved by the engineer and done under AWS D1.4; one cited figure puts the reduced capacity at 35-40% of original.
facts.note: Card says 35-40%. The weakening effect is real, but the specific percentage could not be confirmed and varies with bar chemistry and welding procedure.

facts.fact: Type III portland cement is high-early-strength cement, used when concrete must gain strength fast, for example to strip forms early or in cold weather; Type I is general purpose, Type II moderate sulfate resistance, Type IV low heat, and Type V high sulfate resistance.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: equipment cost accounting
facts.fact: A separate record for each piece of equipment should track its costs, such as purchase cost, depreciation, maintenance and repair, fuel and operating hours, so equipment rates can be charged to jobs and replacement decisions made.
Dry-pack mortar (a stiff, low-water mix rammed into place) is used to fill joints and spaces such as under base plates, with about 1 in commonly cited as the governing joint thickness.
facts.note: Card says joints for drypack should be at least 1 in thick. Sources differ on whether 1 in is a minimum or maximum for dry-pack versus flowable grout; could not confirm.

questions.q: A notch is needed in the bottom edge of a sawn-lumber floor joist, outside the middle third of the span and away from the bearing. What is the maximum notch depth?
questions.why: Notches away from the ends are limited to 1/6 of the joist depth and are not allowed in the middle third; only end notches may go to 1/4 of the depth.

questions.q: Where collar ties connect opposing rafters, what is the maximum spacing permitted by the IRC?
questions.why: Collar ties must be at least 1x4, in the upper third of the attic, and no more than 4 ft apart, which is every third pair of rafters set 16 in on center.

questions.q: In a crawl space, untreated wood floor joists must be at least how far above exposed ground?
questions.why: Joists closer than 18 in (girders closer than 12 in) to exposed ground must be naturally durable or preservative-treated wood.

questions.q: A 2x4 strut supporting a roof purlin runs down to a bearing wall at a slope of at least 45 degrees. What is the maximum unbraced length of the strut?
questions.why: Purlin struts are limited to 8 ft of unbraced length, spaced no more than 4 ft on center, at a slope of at least 45 degrees.

questions.q: Minimum embedment of 1/2-in anchor bolts securing a sill plate to a concrete foundation is:
questions.why: Bolts must be embedded at least 7 in, spaced no more than 6 ft apart, with a bolt within 12 in of each plate end.

questions.q: High-early-strength concrete must be kept above 50 degrees F and moist for at least how long after placement?
questions.why: High-early-strength concrete needs at least 3 days of curing; ordinary concrete needs at least 7 days.

questions.q: Per ACI 347, what minimum construction live load is added to the slab dead load when designing elevated slab formwork (no motorized carts)?
questions.why: The minimum construction live load is 50 psf (75 psf with motorized carts), and dead plus live load must total at least 100 psf.

questions.q: A slab on grade is 5 in thick. What is the minimum depth for its saw-cut contraction joints?
questions.why: Contraction joints should be at least 1/4 of the slab thickness, and 5 in x 1/4 = 1-1/4 in.

questions.q: What is the nominal diameter of a #6 reinforcing bar?
questions.why: Inch-pound bar numbers give the diameter in eighths of an inch, so #6 = 6/8 = 0.75 in.

questions.q: Weld washers are required when puddle welding steel deck thinner than:
questions.why: Deck thinner than 0.028 in will burn through under an arc spot weld, so a weld washer is used to make the connection.

questions.q: Under the AIA A201 general conditions, unless the contract documents provide otherwise, who secures and pays for the building permit?
questions.why: A201 puts the contractor in charge of the building permit and other legally required permits, fees, licenses and inspections, unless the contract says otherwise.

questions.q: A non-exempt carpenter works 8 hours a day, 5 days a week, and must answer the office phone during a 30-minute clocked-out lunch each day. Under the FLSA, how should the lunch time be paid?
c: It is unpaid because meal periods are never compensable
5 hours at 1.5 times the regular rate
2.5 hours at 1.5 times the regular rate
questions.why: A meal break is unpaid only if the employee is fully relieved of duty; the 5 x 0.5 = 2.5 hours push the week past 40, so they are paid as overtime.

questions.q: Which document proves employment authorization but not identity for Form I-9 purposes?
questions.why: A Social Security card is a List C document and must be paired with a List B identity document; a passport or green card is List A and proves both.

questions.q: How long must an employer keep its OSHA 300 log, 300A summary and 301 incident reports?
c: 5 years after the end of the calendar year covered
1 year after the end of the calendar year covered
3 years from the date of each injury
30 years from the date of each injury
questions.why: Injury and illness records are kept 5 years after the year they cover; the 30-year rule applies to exposure and medical records.

questions.q: What rate of Social Security tax is withheld from an employee's wages (up to the annual wage base)?
questions.why: The employee pays 6.2% and the employer matches 6.2%, for 12.4% in total; 1.45% is the Medicare rate.

questions.q: To be eligible for FMLA leave, an employee must have worked at least how many hours for the employer during the previous 12 months?
questions.why: Eligibility requires 12 months of employment, 1,250 hours in the past 12 months, and 50 employees within 75 miles.

questions.q: Under IBC 2021, swinging doors serving a Group H occupancy must have panic or fire exit hardware when the occupant load reaches:
c: Any occupant load; no threshold applies
questions.why: Group H requires panic or fire exit hardware whatever the occupant load; the 50-person trigger applies to Group A and E spaces.

questions.q: An elevator shaft connects three stories. What is its minimum fire-resistance rating (assuming the floors penetrated are rated no more than that)?
questions.why: Shafts connecting fewer than four stories need 1 hour; four or more stories need 2 hours, and never less than the floor penetrated.

questions.q: Where only one elevator is installed and standby power is required, the elevator must transfer to standby power within what time after normal power fails?
questions.why: A single elevator must switch to standby power automatically within 60 seconds of losing normal power.

questions.q: What is the minimum fire protection rating for a door in a fire-resistance-rated corridor wall?
questions.why: Doors in rated corridor walls need a 1/3-hour (20-minute) rating and must also meet smoke and draft control requirements.

questions.q: What is the minimum clearance between the floor and the bottom of a wall-mounted hand-held portable fire extinguisher?
questions.why: At least 4 in of clearance is required below the extinguisher; the top may be no higher than 5 ft for units of 40 lb or less.

questions.q: A van-accessible parking space served by a 60-in access aisle must be at least how wide?
questions.why: A van space is 132 in wide with a 60-in aisle, or 96 in wide if the aisle is at least 96 in.

questions.q: What is the steepest cross slope allowed on an accessible ramp run or landing?
questions.why: A cross slope of no more than 1:48 lets water drain without making wheelchairs drift sideways; 1:12 is the maximum running slope.

questions.q: Handrails are required on both sides of an accessible ramp run when its rise is greater than:
questions.why: Ramp runs rising more than 6 in need handrails on both sides; circular handrails must be 1-1/4 to 2 in in diameter.

questions.q: A 3/8-in change in level on an accessible route will be beveled. What is the steepest bevel allowed?
questions.why: Changes from 1/4 in to 1/2 in may be beveled at no more than 1:2; over 1/2 in requires a ramp.

questions.q: Midrails, screens or mesh are required in a guardrail system unless there is a wall or parapet at least how high?
questions.why: Intermediate members are needed between the top rail and the walking surface wherever no wall or parapet at least 21 in high exists.

questions.q: An owner holds three separate contracts, one each with the architect, the general contractor, and a construction manager who serves only as the owner's advisor. Which delivery method is this?
questions.why: In agency CM the construction manager advises the owner without taking cost risk, and the owner contracts directly with both the designer and the contractor.

questions.q: Without a geotechnical report, what is the IBC presumptive allowable foundation pressure for sandy gravel or gravel (GW, GP)?
questions.why: Gravels get 3,000 psf, sands and silty/clayey sands 2,000 psf, and clays and silts 1,500 psf.

questions.q: Wall finish is installed over wood furring strips. If the space behind the finish is not filled with noncombustible material, fireblocking is required at what maximum interval in every direction?
questions.why: Concealed spaces behind furred finish must be filled or fireblocked at no more than 8 ft in any direction.

questions.q: What is the minimum depth of a footing below undisturbed ground surface (before considering frost depth)?
questions.why: Footings go at least 12 in below undisturbed ground and also below the frost line unless they are frost-protected.

questions.q: An owner pays a progress payment one day late. The contractor stops all work and walks off the job with no intent to return. Legally, which statement is correct?
c: The contractor has committed a material breach
The owner committed a material breach that justified termination
Neither party has breached the contract
The contractor committed only a minor breach
questions.why: A one-day-late payment is a minor breach that allows only damages; abandoning the job is a material breach by the contractor.

questions.q: In Type I or II construction, a skylight sloped less than 45 degrees from horizontal must be mounted on a curb at least how high above the roof plane?
questions.why: These skylights need a curb at least 4 in high, and in Types I and II their frames must be noncombustible.
